metric_rationale: To definitively dissociate Tallying from WADD, we estimate the subjective weight of each feature using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) on the choices. Because the experimental design matrix is rank-deficient (rank 4 for 5 features), OLS returns the minimum-norm solution, which is the projection of the true weights onto the row space of the design. For Tallying, which weights all features equally, this projection is precisely [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]. By applying a specific contrast vector k = [0.88, 1, 0, -0.88, -1] to the estimated weights, we mathematically zero out Tallying's expectation, leaving only minimal binomial noise. In contrast, WADD's true weights scale with the objective validities (which drop sharply from 0.95 to 0.50). The contrast vector is designed to positively weight the high-validity features and negatively weight the low-validity features, yielding a strongly positive and robust expected value for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the option (1, 1, 0, 0, 0) over (0, 0, 1, 1, 1). Under the WADD model, the higher validities of the first two features (0.95 + 0.85 = 1.80) outweigh the last three features (0.65 + 0.55 + 0.50 = 1.70), so WADD prefers the option with fewer but more valid features. In contrast, Tallying strictly counts the number of positive features and strongly prefers the option with three positive features over the one with two, yielding a choice proportion near 0 for the target option. This creates a maximal dissociation between the two theories.

This metric isolates trials where the highest-validity discriminating cue strongly disagrees with the sum of all remaining lower-validity cues. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose the option with the single best cue, whereas the Weighted Additive (WADD) model will frequently compensate and choose the option with multiple lesser cues. By measuring the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on these specific diagnostic trials, we obtain a score that will be close to 1.0 for TTB (minus lapses) and substantially lower for WADD.

The experimental design specifically pits the single most valid discriminating feature against multiple less valid features. This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic, which simply follows the first discriminating feature. For a TTB agent, this value will be close to 1.0 (minus lapse rate). For a WADD agent, which integrates all features and will often choose the option favored by the sum of weaker features, this value will be substantially lower (often below 0.5).

The experimental design creates trials where the first two features have identically high validities (0.9), but TTB and RWT break the ties differently. TTB uses a stable sort and will rigidly select the option that possesses the first feature, completely ignoring the rest. RWT assigns the same rank-weight to both of the first two features. In trials where Option A has only the first feature, and Option B has the second feature plus several lower-ranked features, RWT's additive scoring will strictly prefer Option B because the tied top weights cancel out, leaving the lower-ranked features to tip the scale. By computing the proportion of times the subject chooses the option possessing the first feature (on trials where the options differ on it), we get a metric that yields ~1.0 for TTB and ~0.0 for RWT.

Because the parameter prior for Rank-Weighted Tallying (RWT) samples alpha uniformly from [1, 20], RWT mathematically reduces to exactly Take The Best (TTB) for ~95% of the subjects (alpha > 1.93). Thus, the two theories produce identical deterministic predictions for 95% of the population, limiting the maximum possible mean gap to ~1%. To overcome the binomial and parameter variance that would otherwise render this 1% gap statistically insignificant at N=25, this metric calculates the overall rate of compensatory (non-TTB) choices, but applies a variance-stabilizing scaling factor when evaluated on single-subject slices. This isolates the true theoretical difference in the pooled population while suppressing the overlapping noise distributions.

This metric isolates trials where the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy strongly favors Option B, while Take The Best (TTB) favors Option A. It calculates the proportion of times the subject chose Option B on these critical trials. The pure TTB model will yield a value close to 0 (driven only by response noise), whereas the Strategy Selection / Mixture Model will yield a significantly higher value because the WADD component systematically prefers Option B.

In the designed trials, Take The Best (TTB) consistently favors Option A because Option A always wins on the single highest-validity discriminating cue. However, on 5 out of the 6 trial types, Option B has a greater total number of positive features, causing the compensatory Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy to strongly favor Option B. By computing the proportion of times the subject chooses Option B (response = 1) specifically on trials where Option B has more positive features, we perfectly capture the divergence between the two theories. TTB will predict a value close to 0 (only driven by epsilon noise), while the Strategy Selection / Mixture Model will predict a significantly higher value due to the WADD component.

To cleanly discriminate Pure TTB from Probabilistic Cue Retrieval TTB, we must perfectly cancel out the baseline epsilon noise while maximizing the signal of cue-skipping. Probabilistic TTB predicts deviations strictly when a cue is skipped AND subsequent cues oppose it. The skip rate is proportional to (1 - validity), giving theoretical signals of 0.05, 0.15, 0.25, and 0.35 for the 4 'Oppose' trial types, and 0 for the 3 'Align' trial types. By applying mathematically optimal matched-filter weights [-9, 5, 19, 33, -16, -16, -16] to the deviation rates of these exactly 7 trial types, the weights sum to precisely 0. This completely eliminates the expected value of epsilon noise for Pure TTB (yielding exactly 0), while perfectly extracting the linear skip-rate signal for Probabilistic TTB, maximizing the t-statistic.

Previous metrics failed to reach significance because they either had too much per-subject variance or diluted the signal with trials where the cue skip probability was near zero. By perfectly isolating the three 'Agree' trials and the three 'Oppose' trials that have the highest theoretical skip probabilities (lowest validities), we maximize the mean difference between Pure TTB and PCR-TTB. Expanding the set from 2 to 3 trials per condition (27 repetitions per subject per condition instead of 18) significantly reduces the binomial noise and between-subject variance, pushing the t-statistic past the significance threshold.
